820.title: Hasan the peacemaker
820.hook: the elder grandson, who would one day make peace to spare blood
820.howItsDone: Muslims honor al-Hasan ibn Ali as the Prophet's grandson; Twelver Shi'a Muslims count him as the second Imam, and his settlement is cited as an example of choosing peace to spare lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Fatimah's hands, the mill, the water skin, and words for bedtime. Your line was better than a servant.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is on the pulpit in Medina, speaking to the people. Beside him is a boy: al-Hasan, the son of Fatimah and Ali, his grandson. As he speaks, he keeps turning, one look to the crowd, one look to the boy. Then he says something about the child that nobody in the room can check. It's a prediction, and it won't come true for years. A companion named Abu Bakrah remembered it, and passed it on. Today: Hasan the peacemaker.
screen: `A BOY BESIDE HIM ON THE PULPIT.` → `ONE LOOK TO THE CROWD, ONE TO THE BOY.` → `A PREDICTION.`

segments.voice: Here's what he said, in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari: this son of mine is a sayyid, a leader, and perhaps God will make peace through him between two great groups of Muslims. Perhaps. He doesn't say how, or when. The same report, told by the scholar al-Hasan al-Basri, jumps forward to the grown man. After the death of his father Ali, Hasan led battalions against Mu'awiyah that the narrator describes as like mountains. One of Mu'awiyah's own men warned that those battalions would not turn back before they had killed their opponents. Then messengers went between them with terms, and Hasan accepted. He stepped back from rule, and the two armies did not meet in that battle. Al-Hasan al-Basri then adds the old memory: I heard Abu Bakrah say he saw the Prophet on the pulpit with Hasan beside him. Sunni and Shi'a Muslims read this moment in different lights, and both honor him. In Sunni teaching the hadith is read as fulfilled, and his choice is praised. In Twelver Shi'a teaching Hasan is the second Imam, and the treaty is understood as a hard choice made to protect the believers' blood. Either way, the picture is the same: a man with an army, and a claim, who could have pushed on, and chose the settlement instead. The Arabic word for that kind of peace is sulh: a settlement, a making of peace between two sides. Winning would have had a cost counted in lives. He chose not to pay it.
screen: `THIS SON OF MINE IS A SAYYID.` · `TWO ARMIES LIKE MOUNTAINS.` · `HASAN ACCEPTS THE TERMS.` · `SULH: A SETTLEMENT BETWEEN TWO SIDES.` · then, large: `PEACE THROUGH HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a disagreement that's still open, notice the part of you that wants to win it, and ask what a sulh would look like: not surrender, but a settlement where each side gives something. Find the one thing you could give up, and hold it loosely. If you pray, ask God to make peace through you; if not, just rest with the thought of the argument ending.
Sulh, a settlement, the peace Hasan chose over battle when he stepped back from rule rather than pay for victory in lives. Today's word.
Your line: the peacemaker. A settlement can be worth more than a win. Until tomorrow.

821.title: Husayn, from me
821.hook: the younger grandson: Husayn is from me and I am from Husayn (Tirmidhi)
821.howItsDone: Muslims honor Husayn as the Prophet's beloved grandson; Twelver Shi'a Muslims count him as the third Imam and mourn his death at Karbala in gatherings during the month of Muharram, especially on Ashura.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hasan the peacemaker, who accepted a settlement instead of a battle. Your line was the peacemaker.

A group of companions is walking to a meal they've been invited to. Up ahead, in the lane, a little boy is playing. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, sees him and walks out in front of everyone with his arms wide open. The boy darts this way, then that way. The Prophet follows him, making him laugh, until he catches him. Then he holds the boy's chin in one hand, the back of his head in the other, and kisses him, with the companions watching. The boy is Husayn. Today: what his grandfather said next.
screen: `A BOY PLAYING IN THE LANE.` → `ARMS WIDE OPEN.` → `HE CATCHES HIM, AND KISSES HIM.`

segments.voice: The companion who tells this, Ya'la ibn Murrah, remembered the words that followed, and they're kept in the collection of al-Tirmidhi. Husayn is from me, and I am from Husayn. God loves whoever loves Husayn. Look at the order of that first sentence. Husayn is from me: a grandson comes from his grandfather. Then it turns around. I am from Husayn, as if the grandfather, too, belongs to the child. Muslim commentators have explained the line in more than one way: some as pure closeness, two people who can't be pulled apart; others, especially in Shi'a teaching, as a sign that the Prophet's message would be carried on through Husayn. Either way, it's said out loud, in the street, with the companions listening. Another report, in Bukhari, sets a different habit beside it. The Prophet kissed his grandson Hasan, and a chief named al-Aqra' ibn Habis, sitting there, said: I have ten children, and I have never kissed one of them. The Prophet looked at him and said: whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy. A leader of the community, chasing a small boy through a lane, then saying in front of everyone: this child is from me, and I am from him. Husayn grew up, and his life ended at Karbala; Muslims, Shi'a Muslims in particular, mourn him there, and that is a story for its own day. Today belongs to the boy in the lane, laughing, caught.
screen: `HUSAYN IS FROM ME.` · `AND I AM FROM HUSAYN.` · `TEN CHILDREN, NEVER KISSED ONE.` · `NO MERCY SHOWN, NONE RECEIVED.` · then, large: `GOD LOVES WHOEVER LOVES HUSAYN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child, your own, a niece or nephew, a neighbor's kid, or the child you were, running in a lane. In your mind, open your arms, go after them, let them laugh, and say silently what he said: you are from me, and I am from you. If you pray, ask God's mercy for that child; if not, just hold them close in your mind.
Husayn. The Prophet's grandson, son of Fatimah and Ali, of whom he said: Husayn is from me, and I am from Husayn. Today's word.
Your line: from me. A grandfather who chased, caught, and said it out loud. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

822.title: The people of the house
822.hook: Muslims pray for the Prophet's family in their prayer
822.howItsDone: Muslims say the salawat, the blessing on the Prophet and his family, in the sitting near the end of the ritual prayer, and often at other times when his name is mentioned; in some gatherings it is said aloud together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Husayn, chased through a lane and caught. Your line was from me.

Near the end of the ritual prayer, Muslims sit, and the words get quiet and personal. They bear witness. They send blessings on the Prophet. And then, in the words he taught, the blessing widens: on Muhammad, and on the family of Muhammad. A grandson in a lane, a daughter at a mill, a boy beside him on the pulpit: all folded into the prayer, said again and again across a day. Today: the people of the house.
screen: `SITTING BACK NEAR THE END.` → `BLESSINGS ON THE PROPHET.` → `AND ON THE FAMILY OF MUHAMMAD.`

segments.voice: It starts with a verse. In Pickthall's translation of Surah al-Ahzab: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." The companions knew how to greet him. They didn't know how to ask blessings. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ka'b ibn Ujrah says they asked the Prophet, peace be upon him, exactly that. He taught them a form that begins, in Arabic, Allahumma salli ala Muhammad, wa ala ali Muhammad: O God, send blessings on Muhammad, and on the family of Muhammad, as you sent blessings on Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim. So the family was in the answer from the start. The phrase ahl al-bayt, the people of the house, comes from the same surah. Pickthall renders it "O Folk of the Household", in a verse that speaks of God wishing to remove uncleanness from them. Who is the household? Here Muslims answer in different ways. In Sahih Muslim, Aisha tells of a morning the Prophet came out wearing a cloak, drew under it Hasan, Husayn, Fatimah and Ali, and recited that verse. Shi'a Muslims hold that these, the people of the cloak, are the household the verse means, with a special and lasting place in guiding the community. Sunni readings include the people of the cloak and also the Prophet's wives, since the verse sits among words addressed to them, and some widen it to his clan. Both love them. Both say their names with honor. And in both, the blessing in the prayer never stops at one name. It goes on: and on his family.
screen: `ASK BLESSINGS ON HIM.` · `HOW? AND ON THE FAMILY OF MUHAMMAD.` · `O FOLK OF THE HOUSEHOLD.` · `WHO IS THE HOUSEHOLD? TWO ANSWERS.` · then, large: `AHL AL-BAYT: THE PEOPLE OF THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: This ends our days on the family: Fatimah, her hands, Hasan and Husayn, and the house they lived in. If you pray, say the blessing he taught, slowly, a few times, and let the second half land: Allahumma salli ala Muhammad, wa ala ali Muhammad. If you don't, let the faces of these days come one by one, a daughter at the mill, a boy on the pulpit, a boy in the lane, and hold one household, remembered with love.
Ahl al-bayt. The people of the house: the Prophet's household, blessed with him in the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: and on his family. One name, and a whole household with it. Tomorrow, Bilal.

823.title: Bilal ibn Rabah
823.hook: freed from slavery, the caller to prayer, whose footsteps were heard in the garden (Bukhari)
823.howItsDone: In mosques a muezzin gives the adhan before each prayer, and Muslims may pray two short voluntary units after making wudu, often called the sunnah of wudu, following this hadith about Bilal.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahl al-bayt, the people of the house, blessed in the prayer. Your line was and on his family.

It's the dawn prayer in Medina, still half dark. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, turns to one man with a question. Bilal, tell me the deed you hope in most, because I heard the sound of your footsteps ahead of me in paradise. This man has come up before. He lay under a rock on the hot sand and said one word: one. He was bought and set free. His voice called the prayer. And now he's asked: what are you doing that no one sees? Today begins a new part, the early believers, and Bilal opens it.
screen: `THE DAWN PRAYER, HALF DARK.` → `WHAT DEED DO YOU HOPE IN MOST?` → `YOUR FOOTSTEPS, AHEAD OF ME.`

segments.voice: Start with today's word. A muezzin, in Arabic mu'adhdhin, is the one who gives the adhan, the call to prayer. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Umar tells how the call began in Medina: the companions talked over how to gather people for prayer, and the Prophet said: Bilal, get up and call to the prayer. So the voice that once said only one, under the rock, became the voice the whole town woke to. That's the public Bilal. The footsteps are about the private one. The report is in Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah. The Prophet asks, Bilal thinks, and he doesn't name the adhan at all. He says: I have done nothing I hope in more than this. Whenever I purify myself, by night or by day, I pray with that purification whatever prayer was written for me. That's it. Wudu, the washing before prayer, then a short prayer nobody asked for. A version in the collection of al-Tirmidhi names it as two units. Not a fast, not a famous act. A habit done in an empty room, so small no one would think to ask about it. And it was heard in the garden. Muslims may pray a voluntary prayer known as the two units after wudu, and this hadith is behind it. A man with a very public job pointed to a private thing he did. The voice is what people remembered. The footsteps are what was heard ahead.
screen: `MUEZZIN: THE ONE WHO CALLS.` · `BILAL, GET UP AND CALL.` · `THE DEED: A PRAYER AFTER WUDU.` · `SMALL, PRIVATE, HEARD AHEAD.` · then, large: `THE FOOTSTEPS OF BILAL.`

segments.voice: If you pray, you can do what Bilal did: make wudu, then pray two short units, with nobody asking and nobody watching. If you don't, wash your hands and face slowly with cool water, then give the next minute to stillness, for no reason anyone else would know.
Muezzin. In Arabic, mu'adhdhin: the one who calls the adhan, as Bilal did in Medina. Today's word.
Your line: the footsteps of bilal. The quiet deed was the one he named. That's day eight hundred twenty-three.

824.title: Salman the Persian
824.hook: who left his fire-temple home searching, served Christian teachers, was enslaved, and found the Prophet ﷺ in Medina
824.howItsDone: Muslims honor Salman al-Farisi as a companion of the Prophet, retell his search as a story of seeking, and remember him in the account of the trench at Medina.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bilal, the muezzin, and a small prayer after wudu that was heard in the garden. Your line was the footsteps of bilal.

A young man in Persia has one job: keep the fire burning. His father, a landowner, loves him so much he barely lets him out of the house, and the household fire, the one his people tend in worship, must never go out. One day the father sends him to the fields. On the way he passes a church, hears people praying inside, and walks in. He stays until sunset. He never reaches the fields. Today: Salman the Persian, who tells his own story.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN WHO KEEPS THE FIRE.` → `HE HEARS PRAYER IN A CHURCH.` → `HE NEVER REACHES THE FIELDS.`

segments.voice: The account comes in Salman's own voice, in the Musnad of Ahmad and in Ibn Ishaq's life of the Prophet. He leaves home for Syria, and attaches himself to Christian teachers, one after another, serving each until he dies. When the last of them is dying, Salman asks: who now? The old man tells him a prophet will appear in the land of the Arabs, in a place of palm trees between two fields of black stone, and gives him signs to look for. So he sets out with traders, who betray him and sell him as a slave. He's sold again, to a man in a town of palm trees. Medina. He's been carried, as a slave, to the place he was looking for. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, arrives, Salman goes to him and watches, testing the signs one by one, and becomes a Muslim. The companions help him buy his freedom. Later, Bukhari tells of a day the Prophet recited a verse about believers yet to come. In Pickthall's translation: "Along with others of them who have not yet joined them." Someone asked who those were. The Prophet put his hand on Salman and said that if faith were as far away as the Pleiades, men from among these people would reach it. Salman's story isn't a straight line. Fire, church, slavery, Medina. Muslims remember him as a seeker, and every stage counts in his telling: the home he left, the teachers who guided him, even the wrong-way road that brought him to the right town.
screen: `FROM THE FIRE TO SYRIA.` · `TEACHER AFTER TEACHER.` · `SOLD, AND CARRIED TO MEDINA.` · `FAITH AT THE PLEIADES.` · then, large: `THE SEEKER.`

segments.voice: Hold one question about faith, or meaning, or how to live, that you haven't settled, without answering it, the way Salman carried the old teacher's signs on the road. Then look back at who has helped you with it so far, a book, a parent, a friend, a stranger, and let each come with thanks. If you pray, ask God to guide you; if not, let the question stay open.
Salman, the seeker who left the fire of his home, served Christian teachers, was sold as a slave, and found the Prophet in Medina. Today's word.
Your line: the seeker. A winding road can still arrive where it was headed. See you tomorrow.

825.title: Abu Dharr
825.hook: plain speaker, critic of hoarded wealth, who walked alone and died alone
825.howItsDone: Muslims remember Abu Dharr al-Ghifari as a companion known for honesty, simple living and concern for the poor, and his reports on treating servants as brothers are taught in lessons on character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Salman the Persian, the fire, the church, slavery, and Medina at last. Your line was the seeker.

An army is on the march, and one camel can't keep up. It's thin and slow, and its rider falls further behind, until the column is gone over the horizon. So he gets down, loads his things on his own back, and walks. Later, the people in camp see a figure coming along the road by himself. Someone says: there's a man walking alone. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says: let it be Abu Dharr. It is. Today: Abu Dharr, the man who walked alone.
screen: `A CAMEL THAT CAN'T KEEP UP.` → `HE WALKS, CARRYING HIS THINGS.` → `LET IT BE ABU DHARR.`

segments.voice: The scene comes from Ibn Ishaq's life of the Prophet, on the road to Tabuk. When Abu Dharr reaches the camp, tradition says the Prophet spoke of him: may God have mercy on Abu Dharr; he walks alone, he will die alone, and he will be raised alone. Abu Dharr was a man of plain words. Bukhari keeps a report from late in his life. A visitor found him living out at al-Rabadha, and asked why. In Syria, Abu Dharr explained, he had argued over a verse. In Pickthall's translation: "They who hoard up gold and silver and spend it not in the way of Allah", followed by a warning of a painful doom. The governor said the verse was about other people. Abu Dharr said: it's about us and them. The quarrel grew and reached the caliph in Medina, and in the end Abu Dharr settled out at al-Rabadha. Yet the same Abu Dharr was once corrected. In another report in Bukhari, he insulted a man by mocking his mother, and the Prophet told him plainly: you are a man with the ignorance of the old days still in you. Abu Dharr took it. Later, someone noticed that he and his servant wore matching cloaks, and asked why. He said the Prophet had taught: your servants are your brothers; feed them from what you eat, dress them from what you wear. So the plain speaker was corrected too, and he wore the correction, quite literally, on his servant's back. Tradition says he died at al-Rabadha, far from the city, with his wife beside him, and was buried by travelers who happened by.

826.title: Ammar ibn Yasir
826.hook: son of Sumayyah and Yasir, forced under torture to speak against his faith, and told by the Prophet ﷺ that his heart was what mattered (16:106)
826.howItsDone: Muslim jurists cite Ammar's story and Qur'an 16:106 for the ruling that someone forced under threat to speak against their faith, while the heart stays with it, is not held guilty, and Muslims remember Ammar with honor among the early believers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Dharr, plain words and a long walk alone. Your line was walked alone.

Medina, the early days. The believers are building their mosque with their own hands, carrying mud bricks to where the walls are going up. One brick each, trip after trip. One man is carrying two at a time. He's covered in dust. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops, and with his own hand brushes the dust from the man's head. His name is Ammar. And back in Mecca, this same man broke. Today: Ammar ibn Yasir, and the heart that held.
screen: `BUILDING THE MOSQUE BY HAND.` → `ONE MAN CARRIES TWO BRICKS.` → `THE PROPHET BRUSHES OFF THE DUST.`

segments.voice: We met his family on an earlier day: his mother Sumayyah and his father Yasir, tortured in Mecca for their faith. Ammar was tortured too, and pushed until he said what his captors demanded, words against the Prophet. A report in al-Hakim says he came to the Prophet weeping, and was asked one question: how do you find your heart? At peace with faith, he said. And he was told: if they come back to it, say it again. Commentators connect this with a verse in Surah an-Nahl. In Pickthall's translation, it excuses the one who disbelieves under force: "save him who is forced thereto and whose heart is still content with the Faith." Both are there: the words forced out of him, and the mercy. Now what came after. The scene with the bricks is in Sahih al-Bukhari: everyone carried one, Ammar carried two, and the Prophet brushed the dust from him. The man who broke under torture did not spend his life as a broken man. He carried double. Another report in Bukhari has the companion Abu al-Darda describing Ammar as the one whom God protected from Satan on the tongue of His Prophet. That's how the people around him remembered him: not by his worst moment, but by what was said over him afterward. Ammar's story doesn't pretend the moment didn't happen. What it refuses is to let that moment define the whole man. The heart held. The rest of him got up, and carried bricks.

segments.voice: This week went from Hasan and Husayn and the people of the house to Bilal, Salman, Abu Dharr and Ammar. Let one moment come back when you gave in or didn't hold, don't argue with it, and ask the question he was asked: how do you find your heart? If you pray, ask God's forgiveness and mercy; if not, set the moment down beside you, and breathe.
Ammar, forced under torture to speak against his faith, told his heart was what mattered, and remembered carrying double the bricks for the mosque. Today's word.
Your line: the heart held. One weak moment is not the whole person. Eight hundred twenty-six days, and counting.
